meta.title: Exam 1: Fields and electromagnets

professor.name: Prof. Ada Lindqvist (persona)
professor.persona: Experimental physicist who builds electromagnets. Socratic, strict on units and stated assumptions, and loves asking *where does the reluctance actually live?*

meta.instructions: Answer every question. Show units and state assumptions in written answers. Rate your confidence honestly. It's how the next exam is planned.

questions.prompt: A 20 cm long air-core solenoid has 400 turns and carries 2.0 A. What is the magnetic field near its center?

options.text: About 5.0 mT
About 50 mT
About 1.6 mT
About 2.5 mT

distractor_notes.B: Taking 20 cm as 0.02 m: a factor-of-ten slip converting cm to m.
distractor_notes.C: Dropping the π in μ_{0} = 4π × 10^{-7} T·m/A.
distractor_notes.D: Half the central value, which is the field at the end of a long solenoid, not at its center.

sources.title: Griffiths DJ. Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed. Cambridge University Press; 2017
sources.note: Section 5.3, Ampère's law and the long solenoid

sources.title: Ling SJ, Sanny J, Moebs W. University Physics Volume 2. OpenStax; 2016

questions.hint: Turns per meter first. And what number does μ_{0} really carry?

questions.prompt: An iron-core electromagnet gives 1.2 T in its gap at 3 A. The steel core saturates near 1.6 T. You triple the current to 9 A. Which prediction is best supported?

options.text: The field triples to about 3.6 T, because B is proportional to current
The field rises only a little above 1.6 T: once the steel saturates, extra current adds field at roughly the air-core rate
The field stays at exactly 1.2 T, because saturated iron blocks any further increase
The field drops, because the extra current heats and demagnetizes the core

questions.explanation: B is proportional to current only while the iron's permeability is high. Near 1.6 T the steel saturates and its relative permeability falls toward 1, so further current adds field only at about the rate of an air-core coil. 9 A gives a field a little above 1.6 T, far short of 3.6 T.

distractor_notes.A: Applies the linear rule beyond saturation: the most common misconception.
distractor_notes.C: Saturation slows the rise; it doesn't stop it. Current still adds field through μ_{0}.
distractor_notes.D: Heating raises resistance, but the core is nowhere near its Curie temperature.

questions.hint: Before choosing, ask what happens to the iron's permeability near 1.6 T, then what is left to carry the extra current's field.

sources.title: Jiles D. Introduction to Magnetism and Magnetic Materials, 3rd ed. CRC Press; 2015

questions.prompt: A C-shaped steel electromagnet (μ_{r} ≈ 2000, iron path 40 cm) has a 4 mm air gap. You want a stronger field in the gap without more current. Which change helps most?

options.text: Swap the core for a steel with twice the permeability
Narrow the air gap, since it holds most of the circuit's reluctance
Lengthen the iron core to add more magnetic material
Rewind the coil with thicker wire, keeping the same turns

questions.explanation: Compare effective lengths: the iron acts like 0.40 m / 2000 = 0.2 mm of air, while the gap is 4 mm. The gap holds about 95 % of the reluctance, so B ≈ μ_{0}NI / g. Halving the gap nearly doubles the field; doubling μ_{r} gains under 3 %.

distractor_notes.A: Feels right because iron is 'the magnetic part', but the iron is already a small share of the reluctance.
distractor_notes.C: A longer iron path adds reluctance, so the field drops slightly.
distractor_notes.D: Thicker wire lowers resistance and heating, but the field depends on N·I, which is unchanged.

sources.title: Griffiths DJ. Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed. Cambridge University Press; 2017
Jiles D. Introduction to Magnetism and Magnetic Materials, 3rd ed. CRC Press; 2015

questions.hint: Turn the iron into an equivalent length of air. Which piece is longer?

questions.prompt: An air-core copper coil dissipates 50 W at 2 A. You need 3× the field from the same coil. Ignoring the rise in resistance as it warms, how much heat does it now dissipate?

options.text: About 150 W
About 100 W
Still 50 W, because the coil's resistance hasn't changed
About 450 W

questions.explanation: For an air-core coil B ∝ I, so 3× the field needs 6 A. Heat P = I^{2}R grows 9×: 9 × 50 W = 450 W. In practice it's worse, since copper's resistance rises as it heats.

distractor_notes.A: Scales heat linearly with current instead of with its square.
distractor_notes.C: Same resistance, but the heat depends on the current squared.

sources.title: Ling SJ, Sanny J, Moebs W. University Physics Volume 2. OpenStax; 2016

questions.prompt: A scrapyard crane lifts steel with a magnet and must drop the load on command. Why is that magnet an electromagnet rather than a permanent magnet?

options.text: Electromagnets are always stronger than permanent magnets
Its field can be switched off to release the load
Permanent magnets lose their magnetism when they touch steel
Electromagnets need no power to keep holding the load

questions.explanation: The deciding feature is control: cutting the current removes the field and releases the load. Strong permanent magnets exist, but they can't simply be switched off.

distractor_notes.A: Modern rare-earth magnets are very strong; strength isn't the reason.
distractor_notes.C: Contact with steel doesn't demagnetize a permanent magnet.
distractor_notes.D: The reverse: an electromagnet needs current the whole time it holds the load.

sources.title: Ling SJ, Sanny J, Moebs W. University Physics Volume 2. OpenStax; 2016

questions.prompt: An iron-core electromagnet has N turns carrying current I, an iron path of length l_{i} with relative permeability μ_{r}, and an air gap g. Derive the gap field B_{g} and explain why B_{g} ≈ μ_{0}NI / g when μ_{r} is large. State your assumptions.

rubric.description: NI = H_{i}l_{i} + H_{g}g, with B continuous across the gap (same area, no fringing), so H_{i} = B / (μ_{0}μ_{r}) and H_{g} = B / μ_{0}, giving B_{g} = μ_{0}NI / (g + l_{i}/μ_{r}).
When l_{i}/μ_{r} ≪ g the iron term drops out, so B_{g} ≈ μ_{0}NI / g: the gap sets the field and the iron mainly guides flux. Valid only below saturation.

questions.model_answer: Take a loop through the iron and the gap: ∮H·dl = NI gives H_{i}l_{i} + H_{g}g = NI. Assume the same cross-section and no fringing, so B is the same in iron and gap. Then H_{i} = B / (μ_{0}μ_{r}) and H_{g} = B / μ_{0}, so B_{g} = μ_{0}NI / (g + l_{i}/μ_{r}). For μ_{r} = 2000 and l_{i} = 0.4 m the iron term is 0.2 mm against a 4 mm gap, so B_{g} ≈ μ_{0}NI / g. This holds only while the iron is below saturation.
questions.alternatives: A reluctance-network argument (R = l / μA, flux = NI / ΣR) earns full credit. Including fringing as a larger effective gap area is fine if stated as an assumption.
